common_name: Bertram Anderson Sedum (Dark Purple-Leaf Dwarf Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring toward the front of a border or rock garden where the low, dusky purple foliage reads well up close.

directions: Bertram Anderson is a compact, low-mounding stonecrop long grown for its smoky purple-gray foliage, a color that intensifies with more sun exposure and cooler nights. Dusky rose-pink flower clusters open above the leaves in late summer, drawing bees and butterflies before fading to a rusty bronze that still looks tidy through fall. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; rich or damp soil causes the low mounds to stretch and lose their compact, tinted form. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to refresh vigor and share starts.

common_name: Jose Aubergine Sedum (Upright Deep Purple-Leaf Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set divisions in spring in well-drained soil; established clumps stay upright without staking and pair well with ornamental grasses.

directions: Jose Aubergine forms a sturdy, upright clump of thick, deep aubergine-purple leaves on matching dark stems, holding its shape through the season without flopping the way some older tall sedums do. Broad, umbrella-shaped clusters of dusky pink flowers open over the foliage in mid- to late summer, aging to mauve and then rusty bronze for lasting fall and winter interest if left uncut. Grow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where the darkest leaf color develops; shade or overly rich soil produces greener leaves and weaker stems. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous and well shaped.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Firecracker Sedum (Cherry-Red Foliage Sunsparkler Groundcover Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring, spacing to let the low mats knit together as a groundcover without crowding.

directions: Firecracker is a low, spreading Sunsparkler-series selection whose small, oval succulent leaves emerge gray-green in spring and deepen to vivid cherry red as the season warms. Dense clusters of hot pink, star-shaped flowers rise just above the colorful foliage from mid- to late summer, adding a second season of interest without disrupting the tidy mounded habit. Grow in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; the brightest red foliage color develops with the most direct sun. It tolerates heat and drought well once rooted in and makes a durable edging or rock-garden groundcover.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information

common_name: Cherry Tart Sedum (Burgundy-Red Foliage Sunsparkler Groundcover Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil; the low mats spread steadily and stay tidy without splitting open in summer heat.

directions: Cherry Tart is a mat-forming Sunsparkler-series sedum with fleshy mint-green leaves that flush a rich burgundy-red through the growing season, giving a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover for hot, dry sites. Large clusters of brilliant pink flowers cover the foliage from late summer into early fall, standing out sharply against the dark leaf color. Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, where the tightest habit and deepest foliage color develop; the cultivar resists splitting open at the crown the way some older low sedums do. It spreads readily by rooting stems and is well suited to edging, pavers, and slopes.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Mountain houseleek is a true alpine species native to rocky slopes of the European mountains, forming tight, densely hairy green rosettes only a couple of inches across that hug the ground in a spreading colony. Short flowering stalks bearing star-shaped, reddish-purple blooms rise a few inches above the foliage in early summer on mature rosettes, which then die back as new offsets take their place. It needs extremely sharp drainage and full sun to stay compact, and is exceptionally cold hardy, tolerating deep winter freezes without protection. Grow in gravelly or rocky soil in troughs, scree beds, or crevice gardens where winter wet can drain away quickly.

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Hairy houseleek forms small, globe-shaped rosettes of gray-green leaves covered in fine hairs, an adaptation that helps reflect intense mountain sunlight and shed excess moisture. The tightly packed, ball-like rosettes spread by offsets into dense mats useful for filling gaps in rock gardens, troughs, and crevice plantings. In summer, mature rosettes send up short stalks of greenish-yellow, star-shaped flowers before dying, leaving the surrounding offsets to fill in. Grow in lean, sharply drained gritty soil in full sun; it is fully hardy but rots quickly if the crown stays wet through winter.

common_name: Jade Rose Hens and Chicks (Burgundy-Centered Jade Green Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Jade Rose forms handsome rosettes with a rich burgundy-red center that shades out to jade green at the leaf tips, with fine hairs fringing each leaf edge for extra texture. Rosettes can reach up to five inches across at maturity and multiply steadily by offsets, with overlapping clumps forming an undulating, tapestry-like mound over time. Full sun for at least six hours a day brings out the strongest color contrast between the burgundy centers and green edges; shaded plants fade toward plain green and stretch. Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil in rock gardens, troughs, or green roofs, and avoid any spot where water stands around the crown.
